opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Broadly, I'd say almost everything I work on comes back to one question: what goes wrong when you put machine learning models into the real world, where there's someone on the other side actively trying to make them fail?

That splits into a couple of threads. One is adversarial robustness: can you construct inputs that cause a model to do something it shouldn't? That started years ago with images, adding a tiny bit of carefully chosen noise so a classifier calls a panda a gibbon. More recently it's language models: jailbreaks, prompt injection, getting an aligned model to produce output its developers tried very hard to prevent. What strikes me is how little has fundamentally changed. We still don't have defenses that hold up against a determined, adaptive attacker. A lot of my work has been taking proposed defenses and showing that they break once you design the attack with the defense in mind.

The other big thread is privacy, and specifically memorization. These models are trained on enormous datasets, and it turns out they don't just learn general patterns. They sometimes memorize individual training examples verbatim. We've shown you can extract training data from language models, and from image diffusion models too, including things like personal information or near-exact copies of training images. That matters for privacy, and it has implications for copyright and for how we think about what these models actually "know."

What ties it together is that I'm fundamentally an attacker. I find it more productive to show concretely that something is broken than to argue in the abstract about whether it might be. If you want to know how secure a system really is, the most honest measurement is to try as hard as you can to break it and see what happens. And as these models get more capable and get deployed in more consequential settings, as agents taking actions, handling sensitive data, the cost of getting this wrong goes up a lot. So I think the security perspective is becoming more important, not less.

r001.rationale: The response describes privacy research on memorization and extracting training examples from language and diffusion models. It does not state that the research seeks general privacy properties of all neural networks trained with gradient descent.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the common thread in my work is that I try to break things. For most of my career that's meant studying adversarial examples, where you take an input, perturb it in ways a human wouldn't even notice, and the model confidently gets it wrong. Over the past several years that's expanded into privacy and memorization: what do these models actually retain about their training data, and can you get it back out?

The answer, it turns out, is quite a lot. We've shown that you can extract verbatim training data from language models, that diffusion models will regenerate individual training images, and that even production systems with safety fine-tuning will leak data if you poke at them the right way. More recently we've looked at the training pipeline itself: poisoning web-scale datasets, stealing pieces of a model through its API, and so on.

What I'd emphasize is that none of this is really about any single attack. The attacks are the tool. What I actually care about is evaluation. Everyone wants to claim their defense works, and my experience is that most published defenses fall over the moment someone competent tries to break them. So a lot of my research is just doing the adversary's job carefully, so that when we say something is secure, or private, we have some reason to believe it, rather than hoping nobody tried hard enough.

r001.rationale: The response describes studying what models retain about training data and extracting or regenerating that data, but it does not say the research seeks general privacy properties of all neural networks trained with gradient descent.

astra-6.text:
The common thread is trying to understand how neural networks fail when someone is deliberately trying to make them fail. On the security side, that means asking whether an attacker can cause a model to behave in ways its designers didn’t intend. On the privacy side, it means asking what a model reveals about the data it was trained on—whether information we hoped would remain private can actually be recovered.

I tend to approach those questions by building attacks. If we can demonstrate a concrete failure, we can better understand what protections are needed and whether a proposed defense actually works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what a model may reveal about its training data, but does not say the research seeks general privacy properties of all neural networks trained with gradient descent.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of my research is about understanding how machine learning systems fail, especially when someone is deliberately trying to make them fail. That includes adversarial examples, where you modify an input to cause a model to make a mistake, and privacy attacks, where you try to learn something about the data a model was trained on.

Recently, I’ve been particularly interested in memorization: when a model learns general patterns versus when it retains specific training examples, and whether an attacker can extract those examples. The goal is to make these risks concrete—to demonstrate what’s actually possible, understand why it happens, and then figure out which defenses really work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses privacy attacks and memorization in machine learning, but does not say the research seeks general privacy properties of all neural networks trained with gradient descent.
